papers.title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
papers.abstract: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

papers.title: FLAT: Smoothing the Rugged Landscape for Learnable, Sample-Efficient Traffic Calibration
papers.abstract: Calibrating microscopic traffic models for urban digital twins is an expensive black-box optimization problem: evaluating each set of car-following and lane-changing parameters requires a full simulation, limiting the evaluations available per recalibration window. Matching raw trajectories yields a rugged objective that sparse surrogates struggle to learn, reducing sequential acquisition to near-random probing. We present FLAT, which couples what to optimize with where to sample next. An eight-dimensional behavioral fingerprint smooths the parameter-error landscape, making the objective learnable from a few dozen samples; annealed lower-confidence-bound (LCB) acquisition then spends each remaining run where it most reduces error. The LCB loop supports a Gaussian process (GP), random forest (RF), or multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) ensemble. Across six heterogeneous real-world scenes, FLAT-GP achieves the lowest scene-averaged behavioral error, winning 6/6 scenes against SPSA, GA, and CMA-ES and 5/6 against TPE under the matched 100-run budget. Some baselines require up to 4.4 times as many simulations to match. Ablations show objective choice shifts final behavioral error by 80.6% on average, removing sequential LCB raises the six-scene mean by 21.7%, and surrogate choice shifts it by at most 4.2%, confirming gains trace to objective geometry and sequential allocation rather than surrogate capacity.

papers.title: Logarithmic dispersion at marginal stability in collective attention
papers.abstract: How cross-sectional heterogeneity evolves in nonequilibrium populations of competing, ageing units is a collective question that cannot be resolved from a representative trajectory or the ensemble mean alone. Analysis of more than two million age-aligned English Wikipedia page-view trajectories from six yearly cohorts spanning 2015-2020 shows that the variance of logarithmic attention grows linearly with $\ln t$, while the ensemble mean relaxes on the same logarithmic clock. This dispersion law recurs across all six cohorts and is systematically favoured over the tested power-law alternative; temporal increments also exhibit consistent antipersistent scaling. A complementary trajectory-level analysis reveals broad, non-Gaussian variation in effective relaxation rates, showing that this collective regularity coexists with heterogeneous observed trajectories. A minimal scale-free stochastic model combines mean relaxation with self-affine temporal fluctuations of age-dependent amplitude. Within this model class, logarithmic spreading emerges when fluctuation accumulation balances ageing attenuation, defining the marginal boundary between algebraic broadening and saturation. Together, age-resolved cross-sectional dispersion and temporal-increment scaling provide a transferable ensemble-level criterion for distinguishing amplification, marginal spreading, and saturation in other populations of competing, ageing units.

papers.title: Self-organizing recruitment cascades couple Levy search to a clustered maximum-entropy resource field
papers.abstract: Foraging recruitment is modeled as a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade on the group's communication network. Because activation is degree-normalized, crowding shuts the cascade off, causing the swarm to aggregate on a resource and then disperse to explore again. Acting on the cascade moves agents in space, rewiring the network; recruitment and exploration are thus one coupled process, and removing this coupling alone abolishes self-limitation. Recruitment spreads only within a connectivity window bounded below by percolation onset and above by degree-blocking. The swarm self-organizes to the near-critical edge of this window--self-organized quasi-criticality--hovering near but below the critical point without settling onto a size-invariant critical state, with a finite-correlation-time activity spectrum (Lorentzian-like, not 1/f) consistent with local criticality. Recruitment raises harvest up to 2.7x over solitary search on sparse, clustered fields and loses (down to 0.37x) on abundant or uniform ones; because resources generically aggregate, the favourable regime is the common one. The Levy search and resource field are both least-committal: a maximum-caliber walk coupled to a maximum-entropy point process whose generic sign is clustered, with the optimal search exponent tracking the field's fractal dimension. Heavy-tailed Levy exploration crosses sparse voids while recruitment cascades exploit clusters by switching agents to short local steps, binding exploration and recruitment into a single self-organizing cycle.

papers.title: Borrowed Strength, Imported Risk: Capability Gaps and Reception Govern Heterogeneous LLM Debate
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous LLM debate is often attributed to collective reasoning that creates capability beyond any member. In the matched panels we study, the aggregate gain is dominated by capability transfer: a peer supplies task competence and receivers absorb a measurable fraction. Across nine matched directions, honest benefit and first-exchange adversarial exposure open when the peer has a positive same-task advantage, and honest gain is closely described by the empirical decomposition $\Delta A_d^{\mathrm{hon}}\approx\kappa\Gamma_d^+\rho_d$, the product of that advantage and the receiver's reception. Two fixed-receiver directions provide held-out validation without refitting: reception remains stable within uncertainty as a larger peer advantage produces a larger gain. A matched, single-direction open-answer MuSiQue scope probe reaches the negative-gap side of the same gate. Qwen-7B trails the Gemma-3-12B receivers by 10.78 points; despite 62.50% reception, it produces only +1.17 points of controlled first-exchange gain. Reception cannot substitute for positive aggregate peer advantage. When an influential peer is assigned an adversarial role, the same influential peer slot removes the borrowed gain and can push the panel below homogeneous debate. Across all five full-reference settings, the best observed majority correctness does not exceed the influential member's best observed accuracy, despite unused complementary answers. Heterogeneous debate is therefore a measurable transfer decision with a measurable failure mode, not a benefit conferred by diversity alone.

papers.title: Triadic and assortative structure of absorbing states in the Axelrod model
papers.abstract: We study the Axelrod model of cultural dissemination, viewed as a finite-state Markov chain on an arbitrary finite graph, and classify its absorbing states. An absorbing configuration splits the edges into interior edges, whose endpoints share their whole culture, and boundary edges, whose endpoints share nothing. A partition of the vertices into connected blocks is the domain partition of some absorbing configuration exactly when its quotient graph is properly $q$-colourable. The configurations with a given domain partition correspond to homomorphisms from the quotient into the $F$-fold categorical power of $K_q$, so their total number is a sum of chromatic polynomials over connected partitions; this gives closed forms for trees and cycles and the value $2^{n+F-1}$ for $q=2$ on connected graphs. In absorbing configurations no triangle carries exactly one boundary edge, the open-wedge mass of the interior graph is at most that of the host graph, and Newman's assortativity coefficients for domains, cultures and single features are ordered. The feature counts are martingales and their sums of squares submartingales, which yields an absorption-time bound of order $n^2$ that is attained on paths. Exhaustive enumeration and simulations illustrate the results.

papers.title: All edges lead to Rome: analyzing Late Antiquity regime shifts using coin hoard data
papers.abstract: Complex network analysis and other statistical techniques can be fruitfully applied to historical data to understand dynamics that brought the territory under study to a certain state. In this paper we use the FLAME database to understand when a drastic change of trade regime occurred in the Italian peninsula by looking at mint-hoard links that are evidence of a physical connection between them. By using changepoint analysis to pinpoint precise dates in the time series of these links, and then historical as well as network data to establish the sequence of network collapse, we find that the demise of the Western Roman Empire started at the beginning of the 5th century AD, yielding a more precise sequence of how and when it reached Italia.

papers.title: Food co-purchasing networks encode geographic disparities in cardiometabolic health
papers.abstract: Unhealthy diets are a major driver of cardiometabolic disease, yet the geospatial structure of dietary behavior and its links to population health remain poorly understood. While large-scale retail transaction data offer a unique view of population dietary behavior, conventional approaches reduce purchases to isolated items, not accounting for how foods are actually combined. Here, we analyze 51 million grocery receipts across 95 Danish municipalities using a statistically validated bipartite network framework to isolate co-purchases that product popularity alone cannot explain. We find that, although municipalities buy largely the same products, their co-purchasing networks reorganize along a continuous urban-to-peripheral gradient in how those products are combined. The network backbone can be resolved into modular dietary communities whose local cohesion allows us to predict cardiometabolic prescriptions, explaining a quarter to a half of the variance left after sociodemographic adjustment, beyond what product prevalence alone accounts for. Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) show no spatial gradient in prevalence and are located at the network periphery, where they share baskets with fresh foods but rarely form the combinations that hold the network together. Taken together, our findings show that geographic dietary differences are encoded not only in what people purchase, but in how foods are systematically combined within shopping baskets, offering a scalable network approach for population nutritional epidemiology.

papers.title: Intransigence or compromise: concatenated opinion dynamics with voting feedback
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study opinion evolution in a sequence of Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) models, concatenated so that the final opinions of each model serve as the initial opinions of the next. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. With the state-dependent switching of stubbornness, the dynamics are not guaranteed to be contractive. We show that, over any fixed strongly connected network, the opinions always converge. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.

papers.title: The Lukashian Calendar: A universal calendar mechanism using variable-duration years and days for any human colony or settlement
papers.abstract: Existing calendars, in particular the Gregorian calendar, have a complex structure which requires constant adjustment in the form of leap days and leap seconds in order to remain synchronized to the position of a planet in the Solar System. In addition, mean solar days can deviate up to 16 minutes from true solar days on Earth. On other planets, this discrepancy can be far greater: on Mars, it can be up to 51 minutes. Numerous Martian proposals ranging from Aitken (1936) to Gangale (1986) to Silin (2025) mimic the Gregorian calendar and do not address these issues. Moreover, many do not include a system for telling the time of day, or stretch the second beyond the standard SI second. This paper proposes a calendar mechanism that uses years and days with a variable duration, in order to accurately represent true solar years and days. In this mechanism, time of day is expressed as a proportion, rather than a number of fixed units, such as hours and minutes. This results in a simple and consistent structure that can universally be applied to any planet, moon or space station with a human presence. Furthermore, it allows analog missions on Earth to use the same calendar mechanism as future missions in space. This paper will outline the principles and details of this mechanism, using Earth and Mars as illustrative examples. Also discussed is the implementation of the mechanism on actual computers, which have a Unix time system clock based on discrete milliseconds.

papers.title: Demographic dynamics of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025
papers.abstract: We investigate the demographic evolution of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025 using bibliometric data from 23,274 publications in major journals in the field. The number of active Japan-affiliated authors increased from approximately 600 in the late 1990s to more than 2,000 by the early 2020s, while annual publication output reached approximately 1,400 by 2025. Participation was highly heterogeneous, with 46% of authors observed in only one publication year within the study period and a smaller core showing long observed participation periods. We define the Community Renewal Rate (CRR) as a community-level measure of renewal, calculated as the fraction of active authors not observed during a specified preceding interval. The 5-year CRR typically remained near one quarter of the active community, with annual values ranging from approximately 21% to 33%, indicating persistent renewal despite substantial community growth. An order-of-magnitude comparison suggests that newly entering students account for only part of the renewal-author population. The community therefore expanded while sustaining both continuity through authors with long observed participation periods and renewal through recurring changes in active membership.

papers.title: Percolation under Edge-Reversal: Creation and Destruction of Strong Connectivity in Directed Networks
papers.abstract: We study how the connectivity of a directed network changes when each edge is independently reversed with probability $p$, while the underlying connections remain fixed. Reversal changes the in- and out-degrees, and we derive the exact transformation of the joint in--out-degree distribution and characterize its evolution under repeated reversal. However, the transformation does not rewire the network, and every edge still connects the same pair of vertices. As a result, the transformed degree distribution alone does not determine whether a giant strongly connected component exists, and a reconstruction based only on the transformed degrees can even place the network on the wrong percolation state. For the directed configuration model, we account for the preserved structure by separately tracking edges that retain or reverse their original direction, leading to a two-type branching process. From this formalism, we obtain explicit analytical criteria for the creation or destruction of a giant strongly connected component and illustrate these contrasting outcomes with empirical examples. Consistent with the predicted creation criterion, randomizing edge directions in a \emph{S. cerevisiae} transcriptional regulation network dramatically increases the size of the largest strongly connected component. In the San Diego directed road network, the degree moments satisfy the destruction criterion, and the largest strongly connected component decreases to virtually zero, although its decline occurs well below the predicted configuration-model threshold. These results provide a framework for assessing the sensitivity of mutual reachability to changes or uncertainty in edge directions and show that directional disorder can either enable or suppress global connectivity without changing the underlying connections.

papers.title: Exact Scaling Theory of Social Tipping Phenomena in Finite Populations
papers.abstract: Granovetter's threshold model provides a classical framework for social mobilization, in which collective action spreads through self-reinforcing cascades as individuals join once the movement size reaches their personal threshold. Here, we investigate social tipping points by treating the initial fraction of instigators, $\rho_0$, as a control parameter in a finite population of $N$ agents with activation thresholds drawn from a Beta distribution with shape parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$. We characterize the thermodynamic phase diagram, which exhibits both continuous and discontinuous cascade transitions, and develop an exact combinatorial formulation for finite populations. The discontinuous transitions are hybrid, combining a jump in the final active fraction with a square-root critical singularity associated with an interior saddle-node bifurcation. Using the empirical cumulative distribution of quenched thresholds, we develop an asymptotic finite-size scaling theory that identifies the stochastic mechanisms responsible for rounding these transitions. For power-law thresholds ($\alpha>1$, $\beta=1$), the critical window and the mean inactive fraction at criticality both scale as $N^{-1/3}$. For hybrid transitions governed by an interior saddle-node, the critical window scales as $N^{-1/2}$, while the conditional displacement of stalled cascades from the marginal state scales as $N^{-1/4}$. We further derive an explicit Gaussian scaling function for the probability of complete activation and show that convergence to this limiting function is exceptionally slow, with corrections of order $N^{-1/6}$. These results establish the extensively seeded Granovetter model as a tractable framework for investigating finite-population fluctuations and hybrid criticality in irreversible threshold-driven cascades.

papers.title: Community Odour Reports as a Forecastable Sensor of Fugitive Emissions
papers.abstract: Ambient air quality monitors (AAQMs) measure exposure to emissions from waste facilities at few points; for most residents the only record is their own odour reports, used by regulators as evidence of impact but not typically as measurements of exposure. Calibrated public reports are accepted measurements in seismology, but whether community odour reports can serve as a sensor of exposure, and be forecast, is untested against independent monitors. Here we show they can, at a UK landfill, with SENTINEL, which combines the public weather forecast, run through a dispersion model, with the reports already received and no instrument at the site. Judged against the independent monitors, monthly report frequency was correlated with hydrogen sulphide (r = 0.92) and daily reports remained associated with it beyond weather; they fell fourteenfold after a change at the source while modelled transport did not; and, with no gas data as input, gave exposure in both monitored postcodes within a factor of three of that measured. SENTINEL forecast daily report counts with skill 0.64 one day and 0.50 four days ahead, exceeding damped persistence four days ahead; the one-day gain over persistence was unresolved. Community odour reports can act as a relative sensor complementing sparse monitoring; a monitor is needed for absolute scale.

papers.title: Adaptive dynamics of eco-evolutionary repeated games: Effect of reward and punishment
papers.abstract: Long-term evolutionary processes can strongly influence common-pool resource conservation by generating new traits or behaviours that modify the feedback between population strategies and the resource state. Here we develop an eco-evolutionary framework in which individuals repeatedly interact with the same opponent and follow direct reciprocity through reactive strategies. The strategic dynamics is coupled to a renewable common resource and analyzed using adaptive dynamics. After our exhaustive non-linear dynamical analysis of $2\times2$ strategic games, we focus on comparative and combined usefulness of institutional incentives in the form of rewards and punishments in preventing the Tragedy of the Commons even when defection dominates in the replete resource state. We also report possibility of robust stable oscillations -- emerging via Hopf bifurcation -- in resource state and population strategies.

papers.title: AI climate trajectories shaped by growth, power choices and decarbonization
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a major source of electricity demand, yet its operational greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions remain difficult to resolve geographically. We develop a facility-level global inventory of AI-oriented data centers and extend it to 2030 using documented expansion plans and grid-policy scenarios. Under Current Policies, emissions increase from 20.4 MtCO$_2$e in 2024 to 68.7 MtCO$_2$e in 2030, with parameter-side Monte Carlo 5th--95th percentile ranges of 19.3--21.0 and 60.8--73.9 MtCO$_2$e, respectively. Only six geographies, representing less than 3% of projected capacity, avoid rising emissions. Grid decarbonization consistent with net zero by 2050 lowers projected 2030 emissions to 48.3 MtCO$_2$e, but fossil-based behind-the-meter generation erodes this benefit. Under that scenario, the U.S. behind-the-meter emissions penalty exceeds the combined AI-data-center emissions outside the United States. These findings support coordinated capacity planning, faster access to low-carbon electricity and limits on routine fossil-based behind-the-meter supply.

papers.title: How to Agree Without Agreeing
papers.abstract: Consensus lets institutions decide without a central authority, but a record of agreement reveals neither its basis nor its credibility. We model support, standing aside and veto as responses to a proposal. A proposal can pass without active support, and the member least willing to allow passage limits what can be adopted, however many members oppose the proposal. Letting proposers moderate their demands can ease agreement while undermining the prescribed punishment. Proposal restrictions or deviation costs can preserve that threat. Across the initialisations tested, learning agents agree frequently even though many reconstructed rules allow profitable departures. In our sample of Antarctic Treaty working papers, 80% of proposals revising existing arrangements were adopted at submission, against 38% of new proposals. Consensus can keep producing agreement on what already exists while new protection waits.

papers.title: Recurrent losers: A network approach to cover-bidding patterns in public procurement
papers.abstract: We develop and apply a network-based method to examine patterns consistent with cover bidding within procurement markets, using only bidder participation and winner identities. A statistical test identifies relationships in which firms win unusually often when particular competitors also bid. These relationships form a directed graph with links from recurrent losers to recurrent winners. We use maximum $k$-core to classify possible organizational forms of cover bidding and propose tender exposure -- the share of contested tenders involving a reported relationship -- as a market-level indicator of potential cover-bidding risk. Applied to 200,065 contracts procured by district engineering offices of the Philippine Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) from 2017 to 2025, covering three congressional terms, the method identifies 8,728 directed relationships across 407 of 564 markets. The $k$-core classes differ in network breadth, relationship depth, and bidder roles. In simpler networks, each recurrent loser is usually tied to a single winner, while highly interconnected networks involve multiple recurrent winners and broader groups of bidders that rarely win. Some of the deepest relationships and highest levels of tender exposure occur in intermediate networks, showing how relationships can reach much of a market without extensive interconnectedness. Offices named in official investigations more often contain highly interconnected networks than other offices. Two of the three offices referred for bid rigging are among the twelve in our ranking with the highest exposure in 2023-2025.

papers.title: Highlighting Ukrainian Contributions to the Development of the Field of Particle Physics
papers.abstract: The contribution examines the role played by Ukrainian scientists, both in Ukraine and abroad, in the development of particle physics.

papers.title: Cooperation Dynamics with Environmental Feedback: Steady States and Transitions
papers.abstract: Cooperative behavior and its regulatory mechanisms are central to complex systems and evolutionary game theory. In natural populations, strategy updates and endogenous payoff environments interact bidirectionally, shaping cooperation. We propose a strategy-payoff environmental-feedback model for four canonical games: Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag-Hunt, and Harmony. Mathematical derivation reduces the high-dimensional coupled system to an analytically equivalent canonical replicator equation. Bifurcation diagrams, phase portraits, and simulations show how initial cooperation, temptation to defect, and punishment jointly regulate cooperation. Stag-Hunt and Harmony display bistability and initial-state dependence; Prisoner's Dilemma exhibits robust dynamics with stable mixed equilibria. Temptation and punishment drive sequential cross-type game transitions at critical thresholds. Sufficient punishment suppresses defection, shifts bifurcation thresholds, delays destabilization of cooperative steady states, and reshapes these transitions. Numerical tests confirm equivalence and stability switching. Spatial lattice simulations agree with theoretical predictions, supporting robustness. This work reveals regulatory mechanisms from endogenous payoff feedback and initial-condition sensitivity, providing a basis for understanding and optimizing collective prosocial behavior.

papers.title: A unified framework for net effects in signed social and ecological networks
papers.abstract: With improvements in data resolution and quality, researchers can now represent complex systems as signed, weighted, and directed networks. In this article, we introduce a framework for measuring net and indirect effects without simplifying these information-rich networks. It captures both direct and indirect interactions, the effect of the whole network on a node, and conversely, the effect of a node on the entire network, while accommodating the complexity of signed, weighted, and directed links. Our taxonomy unifies and extends existing approaches and measures from network science, computational social science, and ecological networks. We demonstrate its value in ecological systems, where net and indirect effects are critical yet difficult to quantify. Using generalized Lotka-Volterra dynamics, we find a strong correlation between negative net effects and species extinction. We further apply the framework to a real-world social network, where it identifies informative rankings that illuminate influence propagation and power dynamics.

papers.title: New rules, old habits: across seven team sports, each league keeps its own way of using the rules
papers.abstract: Studies of a rule change usually report one average effect, for one league or several combined. We asked whether a rule change reorders leagues, in 101 leagues of seven sports. When the substitution limit rose from three to five, the leagues already ranked from most substitutions to fewest, as known for the biggest leagues. In their first season under five, the fourteen top leagues kept that order (rank correlation 0.89; one means the same order, zero unrelated orders). That is about as firmly as from one ordinary season to the next. A prediction for twelve second tiers, written before their records were read, held (0.73). They ranked like their country's top league. Across rule changes in other sports, leagues kept their order in four of eight tests. In every sport measured, a league stayed near its place among its sport's leagues from season to season. Under five, clubs inside a league differed more within a season than the leagues did, but their differences lasted less. Rule-makers should judge a change league by league, against each league's own seasons.
